Sepsis is a condition caused by the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream and the resulting reaction that the body has when trying to fight off the infection. The most common cause of sepsis in dogs is a condition called a septic abdomen. In this condition, there is an infection within the abdominal cavity, which was the origin for the bacteria that entered the bloodstream. The most common reason for an infection within the abdomen is the rupture of an intestine with leakage of the intestinal contents into the abdomen. Septic abdomen is a critical condition that requires emergency surgery to resolve the infection followed by intensive postoperative care to keep the patient stable and treat any remaining infection.Because of the critical nature of septic abdomens, the prognosis associated with the condition is guarded. This highlights the need for improved diagnostic tests and treatments for dogs diagnosed with septic abdomens. The ORBITS study seeks to collect blood samples from dogs diagnosed with septic abdomens as well as healthy dogs to look for blood-based markers that could be used to develop novel diagnostic tests for septic peritonitis. A large number of different canine and human cancers appear to rely on signaling through 2 important cellular pathways; the MAPK pathway and the PI3K/mTOR pathway. The drugs trametinib and sapanisertib, which target signaling through these 2 pathways, appear to have significant antitumor effects both in tissue culture and in mouse models. When these 2 drugs were given to laboratory dogs at the doses we plan to test, they were well tolerated and the amount of drug appearing in the blood was predicted to be enough to inhibit tumor growth. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety, biologic effects, and antitumor activity of combined trametinib and sapanisertib given to dogs with measurable malignant tumors. Your dog will receive trametinib orally once daily and sapanisertib orally every other day. They will be rechecked 6 days, and 2, 4, and 8 weeks after starting then every 4 weeks thereafter, as long as their disease is not worsening and the drugs are well tolerated. Visits will generally take about 1 hour, except for the first visit and the Day 6 and Week 4 visits, which may take several hours or all day. They will be eligible to continue receiving treatment as long as the drugs are tolerated and your dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease is stable or smaller). Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (X-rays, ultrasound). Standard bloodwork and urinalysis measurement will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include periodic extra blood draws to look at the amount of trametinib and sapanisertib appearing in the blood and for changes in other blood markers. The total volume of blood involved in each collection is approximately 5 teaspoons. Before starting treatment and after 6 days and 4 weeks, your dog will have a small sample of tumor tissue removed through a biopsy to look for changes in signaling in the tumor cells, if your dog\u2019s tumor is in a location where it can be biopsied. This helps us know if the drugs are finding their targets in the cancer cells. This biopsy will require short acting sedation, and your dog may receive several days of oral pain medication after the procedure.

Feline atopic skin syndrome (FASS) is a prevalent skin condition in cats characterized by chronic inflammation, itching (pruritus), and discomfort. It often results from hypersensitivity to environmental allergens such as pollen, dust mites, or certain foods. Felines affected by FASS may exhibit incessant scratching, licking, and chewing, leading to secondary skin infections and hair loss. Typical management strategies currently combine allergen avoidance, anti-inflammatory medications, and, in severe cases, immunosuppressive therapy. Topical treatments, such as medicated shampoos or spot-on products, can provide relief for localized symptoms. However, these strategies have limited efficacy or can have significant side-effects. We are now opening a clinical trial for a novel monoclonal antibody (MAB) that targets FASS. It is double-blinded, placebo controlled study. The clinical trial aims to evaluate both efficacy and safety of the MAB in affected felines.

\n

This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of a Vaccine Peptide Library (VPL) when given to dogs with cancer. This clinical trial conducted in pet dogs with cancer is designed to test whether the immune responses generated through routine vaccination against common viruses can be re-directed toward cancer cells. The approach appears to work in mouse models of cancer, and we are interested in evaluating it in pet dogs that have naturally occurring cancers that are very similar to humans. If successful, this research would help develop safe, effective, and low-cost ways of treating cancer that would benefit a wide variety of patients, especially those that live in communities with minimal access to cutting-edge cancer care (such as developing and low-resource countries). Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently open human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent. As part of this study, your dog will be randomized to receive one of two vaccine protocols: either combination treatment with Shingrix/Garadasil vaccines or a rabies vaccine. Your dog will come to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital for the primer phase, which includes 1-3 weekly injections of the vaccines. Two weeks later, they will return to start weekly visits for injection of the VPL directly into the tumor for 8 weeks. Dogs will be treated with diphenhydramine (Benadryl) prior to the injection and then will be monitored for 4-6 hours post-injection. One final visit will be required one week after the last injection (total length of study 12-14 weeks). Physical exam and blood collections for study purposes will be performed at each visit. A complete blood count will be performed every week during the treatment phase; blood and urine for serum chemistry profile and urinalysis will also be collected on Weeks 1, 5, and 9. Chest x-rays +/- abdominal ultrasound will be checked prior to the primer vaccine and at Week 9. Lymph node aspirates for study purposes will be obtained at Weeks 1, 5, and 9 of the treatment phase. Biopsies of your dogs tumor will also be collected prior to the first dose of the drug (pre-treatment), on Week 5, Week 5 at 24hrs, and Week 9 depending on how your dog has responded to therapy. Each of these biopsy sessions will occur under anesthesia, either local (sedation with anesthetic) or general.

\n

First line conventional chemotherapy, Lomustine, provides a response rate of 29% for only a median of 96 days

\n

In this proposed trial, we will investigate a novel drug, Trametinib, to determine the antitumor activity (shrinkage of tumor) of the drug in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma using progression-free survival (PFS).

\n

PFS is defined as the percentage of dogs that are progression-free at 6-months post treatment initiation.

Melanoma is the most dangerous form of skin cancer and kills over 9,300 people a year in the US. Melanoma is also the most common oral cancer in companion dogs and like human melanoma, it is an aggressive cancer that spreads to lymph nodes, lungs, liver, brain, and kidney.

\n

Unfortunately, once melanoma spreads to distant sites, it is usually incurable. Despite advances in standard-of-care therapies (e.g., surgery, radiation therapy (RT) , and chemotherapy), the average survival in dogs with melanoma of advanced stage is less than one year after diagnosis, and less than 6 months if the melanoma has already spread. Therefore, as in human melanoma, new treatments for canine melanoma are needed to improve survival. Treatments that activate the patient's own immune system (immunotherapy) to fight the melanoma have worked very well in some human and dog patients.

\n

We are evaluating a combination of 3 types of therapy all of which have shown immune activation and anti-melanoma activity as single therapies in patients with melanoma. The three therapies include: administration of an immune stimulant directly into the tumor, radiation therapy targeted at the primary tumor, and intravenous administration of an antibody that potentially enhances the body's immune response to the melanoma. We hypothesize that by combining these therapies, we will be able to further extend the life of patients with melanoma.

\n

There are 3 parts to this study: Part 1 has been completed, and we have determined the dose of the immune stimulant to be administered directly into the tumor; In Part 2, the immune stimulant was combined with radiation therapy targeted at the same tumor, and; in Part 3 (Aim 1), the immune stimulant was administered to all sites of palpable disease in addition to the treatments in Part 2. Both Part 2 and Part 3 (Aim 1) are completed.

\n

In Part 3 the immune stimulant is administered directly into the tumor combined with intravenous (IV) Anti-PD1 monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor , [ICI]) and radiation therapy directed at the primary oral tumor. The information from this study will guide further clinical trials in both dogs and humans.

\n

Owner Responsibility\nThe owner is expected to make and keep all appointments according to the study protocol. The pet will receive the first ICI therapy and then will receive the RT treatment 2 weeks later along with the second ICI treatment. Six days after the RT treatment, your dog\u2019s tumor will be injected with the IT-IC treatment for 3 consecutive days. ICI treatments will be given 3 more times at 3-week intervals. The sentinel lymph node (SLN) is the\nprimary lymph node draining the tumour and although one might expect that it is the first lymph\nnode downstream from the tumour, this is not always true. Failure to identify and assess the\nsentinel lymph node can lead to incomplete treatment, worse prognosis and poor patient outcome.\nCurrently in veterinary patients, there are not good protocols in place to identify sentinel lymph\nnodes. The development of these protocols could help us to decrease the number of lymph nodes\nwe remove, in addition to ensuring we are accurately evaluating the most important lymph node\nfor making follow-up treatment recommendations.\n\nYou will be responsible for bringing your pet to the OVC-HSC for both the CT scan and surgery\n(may occur during the same visit). Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is an inherited, slowly progressive heart disease that affects up to 45% of Doberman Pinchers in the U.S. The disease has two phases. In the first phase, dogs do not have clinical signs of DCM, but changes to the heart may be seen by echocardiogram or by measuring electrical abnormalities in the heart. Over time, the disease usually progresses to the second phase, when clinical signs of congestive heart failure such as breathing problems and fainting can appear. DCM can eventually lead to death.

\n

Early identification of DCM is essential, since treatment can delay the onset of clinical signs and prolong the dog\u2019s life. Screening for DCM is crucial not only to identify dogs that are affected by this disease, but to support healthy breeding programs.

\n

Current screening for DCM is costly and time consuming. A significant proportion of affected dogs have heart abnormalities that are not detectable using standard echocardiographic exams. Hence, 24-hour Holter monitor evaluation is used.

\n

Echocardiography-derived speckle tracking (STE) is a newer technique that is rapidly gaining attention for diagnosis of DCM in humans. STE has the unique capability of non-invasively monitoring the heart with minimal additional time or cost compared to current methods. In this study, we\u2019re testing whether STE will be able to detect changes in the hearts of Dobermans who have abnormal 24-hour Holter monitoring but normal standard echocardiograms.

\n

About the study


With the advancements in modern medicine, both humans and canines are living longer and we are now seeing a greater number of dogs suffer from dementia. Currently, there are no approved treatments for cognitive decline in either humans or dogs. This study aims to find a safe and effective drug for reducing progression of the disease. Cannabidiol (CBD), trazodone, and rapamycin have shown beneficial effects on brain aging, which means they may be effective treatment options for dogs suffering from canine cognitive dysfunction (CCD). All three drugs will be tested in order to determine if one, or all, may be a safe and effective medication for reducing the progression of dementia in dogs.


Who qualifies


Dogs who meet the following eligibility criteria will qualify for this clinical trial

  1. Greater than 8 years old
  2. Greater than 20lbs
  3. Show signs of dementia (wandering, confusion, new behaviors)
  4. Otherwise systemically healthy and able to undergo multiple anesthetic events


Study Design


After an initial heal assessment which includes a brain MRI and spinal tap, all clients will go home with a liquid medication to be given twice daily and a pill to be given once weekly. This study is blinded, so pet owners will not know which treatment group their dog is in. All pet owners will be expected to bring their pet back every 3 months over the course of 2 years with an MRI being conducted every 12 months (3 total) and a spinal tap being conducted every 6 months (5 total).


Commitment


This is a 2 year study and it is important to be committed to remaining in the trial for the entirety of the 2 years, unless the pet reaches the end of their life prior to that. Pets will need to come to the VTH for appointments every 3 months and undergo several anesthetic events throughout the study.


In the unfortunate event that a pet reaches the end of their life, the euthanasia and autopsy are required to be performed at CSU. While this is not pleasant for anyone to think about, it is extremely important for the study to be able to analyze these final samples. We will pay for the euthanasia, along with a general or private cremation, depending on the pet owner's preference.


Financial Incentives


All diagnostics, drugs, and exams related to the study will be covered by the study. A $250.00 credit will be applied directly to the pet owner's VTH account every 6 months with continued successful study visits for a total of $1000.00 upon full 2 year study completion.

When patients undergo fractionated radiation therapy, maintaining appetite, consistent stools, and body weight are incredibly important for patient well-being and quality of life. The most common non-radiation complications in dogs undergoing these longer radiation protocols include diarrhea, vomiting or regurgitation, and decreased appetite. When these complications happen in patients, both owners and clinicians attempt to offer a multitude of foods, home cooked diets, probiotics, appetite stimulants, anti-nausea medications, or antibiotics. Recently nutritionists and veterinarians at a well-known pet food manufacturer developed a prescription diet designed to specifically help nourish and support dogs that are fighting cancer. This diet is highly digestible and contains a proprietary blend of prebiotic fibers to help support a healthy gastrointestinal microbiome to provide consistent stool quality. The goal of this study is to evaluate the acceptance of the novel diet through food intake and eating enthusiasm data by dogs undergoing daily, definitive intent radiation therapy, and to examine the differences in body weight changes, muscle condition scoring, body condition scoring, body fat index, quality of life, and stool consistency over time in dogs receiving the novel vs control diet.


If your dog participates in this study, he/she will have blood work, urine panel, fecal analysis, and will be randomized to receive one of the two study foods during radiation therapy. Blood work and fecal analysis will be performed prior to starting radiation therapy, half way through radiation, at the end of the radiation protocol and two weeks after completing radiation. Urine panel will be performed prior to starting radiation, at the final radiation dose, and at the two week recheck. We will assess intake of the diet and enthusiasm of the diet twice weekly. We ask that you also record food intake and eating enthusiasm twice a week, fecal scores at each defecation, and quality of life weekly with provided guides and questionnaires. You and your clinical team will be blinded to which diet your dog is receiving, but this will be revealed at the conclusion of the study period.

About the study


Every year, about 3 out of every 100 dogs will be diagnosed with a brain tumor. Many of these dogs will be diagnosed with a glioma tumor, which is the second most common type of brain tumor and also, unfortunately, the most difficult to treat. One of the most promising developing areas of research for treating glioma tumors is immunotherapy, which is a type of intervention that uses the dog's own cells to fight the cancer cells.


This study is looking at a specific type of immunotherapy called CAR T cell therapy. CAR T cells are created by doing a simple blood draw from the dog to extract the T cells (\"fighter\" cells), which are then infused with a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) protein. This \"upgrade\" allows the T cells to target and attack the glioma tumor cells. This intervention has been used in children with brain tumors but this study will be the first time it's being used in dogs with glioma tumors!


In addition to the immunotherapy, we will be looking at a specific type of chemotherapy that has shown extremely promising results in canine lymphoma, along with human glioma tumors. This chemotherapy drug, verdinexor, will be used in combination with the CAR T cell therapy in an effort to produce the best possible outcome.


Who qualifies


Dogs who are over 10kg (22lb) in body weight who have already had a brain tumor diagnosed on MRI.

Tumor must be surgically accessible to allow for biopsy and injection of CAR T cells directly into the tumor

Dogs must be healthy enough to safely undergo anesthesia for the biopsy of the tumor

Dogs cannot have previously received chemotherapy or radiation for this tumor


Study activities and Timeline


Visit 1 | Day-17

  1. Exam
  2. Blood draw to create CAR T cells
  3. Begin verdinexor (chemo) therapy twice per week

Visit 2 | Days -4 and -3

  1. On both days, we will give a drug that temporarily depletes the immune system to prepare your dog's body for the CAR T cell injection

Visit 3 | Days 0, 1, and 3

  1. The first day will consist of the first CAR T cell injection while the next 2 days consist of recheck exams

Visit 4 | Days 8 - 10

  1. The visits throughout these days will consist of a brief planning scan followed by the brain biopsy surgery. During the surgery, a second injection of CAR T cells will be given directly into the tumor.

Visit 5 | Month 3

  1. We will do a recheck a MRI to evaluate the tumor response


Verdinexor will continue to be given at home twice weekly until the tumor progresses based on neurological signs or growth seen on MRI.

Nasal Cancers in dogs and cats are uncommon and standard treatment is external beam radiation therapy. Side effects from radiation therapy may sometimes be severe and not every patient will qualify or respond to this therapy. Plus, there are significant delays in accommodating patients for timely radiation therapy treatment due to the paucity of centers and available specialists.


Nasal Electrochemotherapy has been used predominantly outside of the United States (see below).


Radiol Oncol 2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430.

 doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec.

Minimally Invasive Electrochemotherapy Procedure for Treating Nasal Duct Tumors in Dogs using a Single Needle Electrode

Felipe Maglietti 1 2 3, Mat\u00edas Tellado 4, Nahuel Olaiz 1 2 3, Sebastian Michinski 1 2 3, Guillermo Marshall 1 2 3


Abstract

Background: Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we use electrochemotherapy (ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors.

Materials and methods: In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.

Results: In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treated nasal passage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively.

Conclusions: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treat nasal tumors with encouraging results.


We now have a nasal electrochemotherapy electrode here in the United States.


Clinical Protocol involves selected patients to receive a short sedation with IV propofol, +/- dexdomitor and O2 via intubation. Bleomycin IV 8 minutes prior to electrode placement into both nares providing a short pulse which opens the cell membranes driving chemotherapy to the region being treated. In this case, we begin treatment at the deepest point of the nasal cavity just proximal to the region of the cribiform plate (end of nasal cavity). After each treatment, the electrode is moved proximally until the entire region of both nasal cavities are treated. No chemotherapies have been FDA-approved for use in cats despite a growing need for such therapies. Paclitaxel (Taxol\u00ae) is one of the most effective anticancer agents used in human cancer therapy today, with potent activity against a variety of cancers in people that also occur in cats. Paclitaxel has been found to kill cancer cell lines isolated from cat tumors in the laboratory, but only one small study has been published evaluating paclitaxel treatment of cats with cancer. In that study, 5 of 9 patients responded to paclitaxel therapy, with 4 of these patients experiencing stable disease and one patient experiencing a partial response. 


The current FDA-approved formulation of paclitaxel for use in people, which uses a cremophor-based agent to solubilize the drug for injection, causes allergic reactions in dogs and cats. This characteristic of the FDA-approved formulation has largely prevented its use in pets. The investigational drug to be used in this study, Paccal\u00ae Vet, uses a formulation that has been created to minimize allergic reactions and therefore improve tolerability. Several clinical trials have been performed or are ongoing with this formulation in dogs, but to date, no studies in cats using Paccal Vet have been undertaken. 


The primary purpose of this study is to test the tolerability of Paccal Vet in cats and to determine an acceptable dose. A secondary, exploratory goal is to see whether Paccal Vet may have anti-tumor activity in various tumors in cats. In this context, \u201cexploratory\u201d means that this study is not large enough to prove whether or not Paccal Vet is working in feline cancer. However, the results could help the drug developer determine whether the drug might have the potential to do so. 


The \u201cinvestigational\u201d part of the study is to test whether Paccal Vet is safe for use in cats and whether the drug may induce an anti-tumor response against their cancer. Paccal Vet is an investigational drug, which means it has not yet been approved by the FDA for use in dogs or cats. The potential benefits and safety of Paccal Vet in the treatment of cats with various cancer types have not yet been demonstrated. The purpose of this study is to test the investigational use of Paccal Vet rather than to provide medical treatment to your cat.


Cats enrolled in the study will receive Paccal Vet via intravenous infusion over 15-30 minutes once every 3 weeks for up to four doses. Throughout those treatment cycles, cats will be monitored carefully for tumor responses and adverse events through physical examinations, blood work, and quality of life questionnaires.

Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that pose significant therapeutic challenges in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by locally invasive growth and poor overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds\u2014particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers\u2014are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy may also be used as a standalone treatment, delivered through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT). SRT offers the advantages of high precision, greater tissue sparing, and shorter treatment duration. Despite these interventions, the prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. Their natural disease course, intact immune system, and clinically comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable for evaluating the efficacy and safety of emerging therapies.

One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy. In this study, we investigate the combination of stereotactic radiation therapy with an FDA-approved nanoparticle, previously shown to be safe in dogs. This nanoparticle has demonstrated the ability in rodent models to modulate the tumor immune microenvironment by transforming tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from an M2 (pro-tumor) to an M1 (anti-tumor) phenotype.

This synergistic approach may not only improve survival in canine patients but also provide critical translational insights for the treatment of glioblastoma in humans.

This is where small incisions are made for cameras and instruments, and tissue can be removed without making a large incision. Our goal is to obtain important cancer care information from SLN mapping, but with the potential benefits of MIS compared to open abdominal surgery.

Purpose

To evaluate the effects of histotripsy, a high-precision ultrasound-based treatment that can non-invasively destroy tumor tissue without radiation or heat, on dogs with oral tumors. 


Background

Histotripsy is an emerging technology that uses focused ultrasound waves to mechanically destroy tumor tissue. Histotripsy has the ability to precisely destroy tumors non-invasively and without using heat or radiation. Histotripsy also has the potential to stimulate the immune system into fighting off remaining or microscopic tumor. Our team\u2019s previous research has evaluated the safety and efficacy of histotripsy for bone tumors, soft tissue sarcomas, and brain tumors in dogs. Additionally, histotripsy was FDA-approved for the treatment of liver tumors in humans in 2023, with promising clinical results. We are now interested in how histotripsy affects oral tumors in dogs. 


Study Design

Dogs will undergo CT and/or MRI scans (if not obtained previously during diagnostics) to visualize the oral tumor and plan the histotripsy treatment. The histotripsy treatment approach will be patient-specific to accommodate for unique tumor sizes and locations.  

On the day of treatment, hair will be removed from the area overlying the tumor to allow for maximum transmission of the ultrasound waves. Histotripsy treatment will be delivered non-invasively through the skin to mechanically disintegrate the underlying tumor. Dogs will be maintained and monitored under anesthesia. After the treatment, images (CT and/or MRI) will be taken to assess the immediate effects of the ultrasound treatment. Most patients recover uneventfully and go home the same day.

One day after the completion of histotripsy treatment, dogs will undergo standard-of-care surgical resection. This allows us to assess the effects of the ultrasound treatment. At this point, participation in the study is complete.

Risks of the surgery include infection, problems related to the implants, and local recurrence. Many factors are contributing to the high rate of complications and one of them is likely the material used to fabricate the implants. We hypothesize that if the implant used to replace the segment of bone with the tumor (i.e. endoprosthesis) was made of a material that the body could replace with its own viable bone, many of the complications would not occur or would be easier to treat.


3D-printing can create personalized implants made of a material that the body can replace with its own bone, namely anorganic (deproteinized) bone mineral (ABM). Over a period of time, the body can grow new viable bone while removing the ABM, such that the metal plate and screws used with limb sparing would be able to be removed after a period of time, leaving the dog with only its own tissues. The goal of this study is to evaluate a novel personalized implant system for limb sparing in dogs with primary bone tumors and identify complications associated with this surgical approach.


Dogs will undergo imaging with a PET-CT scan, which is a special form of imaging that involves giving a small dose of a radioactive substance to help identify any areas of cancer spread. The data from this imaging will also be used to create the patient-specific implant and tools for surgery, which is anticipated to take 5 days or less. Once the supplies are ready, the limb sparing surgical procedure will be performed. Dogs will return two weeks after surgery for suture removal and to start carboplatin chemotherapy as long as the surgical site is well-healed. Carboplatin will be given every 3 weeks for 6 treatments, and dogs will be followed for up to 20 months after surgery. X-rays of the chest and limb will be performed every 8 weeks for the duration of the study, and force plate gait analysis will be done every 6 months. Some of these follow-up visits can be done with your regular veterinarian if you choose; however, the study will not be able to cover the costs of these visits.

Cannabidiol (CBD) is a non-psychoactive phytocannabinoid from the Cannabis sativa plant. It has a wide range of reported physiological and biochemical interactions. Most of these veterinary studies use different formulations of CBD ranging from specific isolates to full spectrum products, with most pharmacokinetic (PK) studies with these formulations being performed on in-bred laboratory animals. An absence seizure disorder has recently been identified in the Cavalier King Charles Spaniels (CKCS) breed, similar to absence seizure disorders seen in people. A wide range of presenting signs have been reported, including myoclonus (\u201chead nodding\u201d), episodes of decreased awareness, sleep disturbances, unexplained behaviour changes, and potentially fly-catching. It is currently unclear how this disorder is best managed. The goal of our study is to identify the most effective medication.


What will happen during this study?

Prior to enrolment, the dog's recent medical records will be screened to assess their eligibility for inclusion. Caregivers will then have a 10-20-minute telephone call with a researcher to help prepare them and their dog for the first visit. At the first visit, enrolled CKCS will undergo a full examination and potentially some blood testing. A 4-5 hour electroencephalogram (EEG) will then be performed by a researcher. If an absence seizure disorder is confirmed by EEG, the dog will be randomly assigned to one of two treatments. Treatments are in the form of an oral capsule, which will be administered twice daily at home for 3 weeks, before a second assessment that includes a repeat EEG. This is a blinded study, meaning caregivers will not know which treatment group their dog was assigned to until the end of their enrolment. Caregivers will additionally be asked to complete a 20-60 minute online questionnaire, both before and after the treatment period.


EEG is considered to be safe and generally well-tolerated. Some dogs may require sedation to facilitate placement of the electrodes. This sedation is then reversed after the electrodes are placed.

The goal of this study is to test whether giving these medications at a special point between the ears (called GV20), instead of by the usual muscle injection, can lower the chance of vomiting while still providing the same level of calming and sedation. Limb sparing is another option but limited in availability and is considered invasive.


Targeted bone electrochemotherapy (ECT-B) is an emerging focused cancer treatment therapy predominantly utilized in people with metastatic cancer to bone as a component of reducing bone pain and retarding tumor growth. It involves the insertion of a single pole electrode into the tumor and drawing chemotherapy directly to the tumor. In addition, once treatment is rendered, the remaining bone defect will be filled via sterile orthopedic bone cement, the patient recovered and discharged the same day.

In the past, osteoarthritis (OA) was thought to be a disease where the smooth cartilage in a joint slowly breaks down. Today, scientists know that OA affects the whole joint, not just the cartilage. This includes the bones, ligaments, meniscus, and the lining of the joint.

Even though doctors can see joint damage, there is a big problem: the amount of damage does not always match how much pain someone feels. Pain can be confusing

and different for each person or animal. For example, two patients\u2014whether they are horses, dogs, or people\u2014can have joints that look the same on X-rays, but one may

feel a lot of pain while the other feels very little. This means that x-ray severity of joint injury does not correlate to the level of pain experienced.

In people, scientists have many ways to measure pain, but in horses this is much harder. We can study how a horse walks and measure lameness using special tools,

but we do not have good, reliable ways to measure how much pain a horse feels. The goal of this study is therefore to use validated pain-testing methods from people and

adapt them for horses, especially for horses with osteoarthritis in the fetlock joint.

Pain has been studied in horses before by looking at things like how they move, how active they are, and their heart rate. However, these behaviors are usually studied one

at a time, and researchers have not always checked how accurate or consistent these

tests are.

This research will study non-invasive tests used in people and see how well they work in horses. The study will focus on three areas: how horses sense pain (Aim 1), how they move (Aim 2), and their activity and natural behaviors (Aim 3).

By doing this, researchers hope to better understand pain in horses and improve how

pain is measured, bringing horse pain research closer to the level used for people.


Procedures

1) Online enrollment survey

2) First Visit \u2013 Veterinary physical and lameness evaluation, including jogging, lunging, x-rays, blood sample and IV sedation if needed

3) Second Visit \u2013 blood sample, hair and fecal collection, heart rate monitoring and ECG collection with equipment, lameness evaluation using videography, continuous activity monitors with GPS sensors, quantitative sensory testing using noninvasive methods, using tactile, vibration, thermal and pressure tests which are routinely used in humans. At this visit, they will also have overnight behavioral observation using an IMU device and video observation.

** at the conclusion of the second visit, some phenylbutazone tablets will be given to the owner to administer before the third visit*

4) Third Visit \u2013 a repetition of the exercises performed at the 2nd visit, now with phenylbutazone on board for the horse to evaluate how this drug modulates the

sensation of pain level in the horse. At this visit, they will also have overnight behavioral observation using an IMU device and video observation.

5) Fourth Visit \u2013 will occur one year after the conclusion of the initial testing and will form a similar visit schedule as during the initial year 1 testing outlined above.

Full-thickness skin grafts are often required for dogs with large or complex wounds. Although these procedures are commonly performed, some grafts fail to fully attach or heal, leading to delayed recovery, additional surgeries, or discomfort for the patients. 


The study investigates whether a placental matrix \u2013 a biologic material rich in natural healing factors derived from bovine placental tissue \u2013 can improve graft success and reduce complications when applied at the time of skin grafting. Placental matrices contain growth factors and structural molecules that may enhance graft adherence, improve blood vessel formation and reduce inflammation within the graft bed. 


Treatment: As part of the standard grafting procedure, your dog will receive general anesthesia. During surgery, a full-thickness meshed skin graft will be harvested from a donor site on your dog and placed over the wound bed. As the research component of this procedure, a single application of placental matrix will be applied topically to the graft surface at the time of surgery. This application is non-invasive, painless, and performed while your dog is already under anesthesia. A non-adherent dressing and bandage will then be applied in a routine fashion. 

Following surgery, your dog will be monitored in hospital for 12-24 hours before discharge. The first recheck visit will occur approximately 5 days after the procedure, with subsequent visits every 3-7 days as determined by the attending veterinarian based on the graft site and any complications. Grafts are anticipated to be healed within 21-30 days on average. At each visit, a brief wound assessment and standardized photographs will be obtained to measure graft healing progress.

Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in dogs, specially in large size breeds and it presents a high biological aggressiveness, in many cases at the time of diagnosis, metastatic dissemination has already occurred. Currently, the standard of care consists of surgical excision of the affected limb, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. However, despite initial therapeutic response, patients develop treatment resistance, leading to the presence of metastasis, most commonly within the lungs, reducing life expectancy and quality of life of the patient. 

Recently the use of liquid biopsies, a minimally invasive sample collection from body fluids, such as blood, has been increasing, as they detect specific molecular biomarkers. Liquid biopsies can aid in the detection of certain pathologies, monitor disease progression or recurrence after the treatment, the latter can be achieved by measuring molecules such as proteins and microRNAs that are in the circulating blood. These proteins and microRNA might provide less invasive and faster detection than other techniques, such as computerized tomography (CT scan). 

For our research the main goal is to determine if this blood test is able to predict osteosarcoma recurrence, as these biomarkers may provide an earlier status of relapse, and could aid in designing more effective treatments. To support this, our team is developing a lab-on-a-chip platform that can measure the selected biomarkers using a minimal volume of blood. To achieve the previous, we are looking for canine patients, over 25 kg (55.11 lbs) that have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma, and have not undergone amputation of the affected limb.

Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.


Dogs enrolled in the study will receive a single intravenous injection of ICG approximately 24 hours before their planned surgery for bladder tumor removal, and a special near-infrared camera will be used during the procedure to assess whether the tumor and its margins fluoresce differently than surrounding normal tissue. ICG is an FDA-approved dye that is commonly used for other imaging purposes in human and veterinary medicine, but its use for identifying bladder tumors during surgery in dogs is considered investigational and its effectiveness for this purpose has not yet been established. A total of five dogs will be enrolled in this study, and all dogs will receive the same dye injection and imaging procedure during their planned surgery; there are no separate treatment or control groups. Study participation is complete after surgery is performed.

Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.


BAQ-13 works by blocking a process called autophagy, which cancer cells use to survive treatment. This study will evaluate whether BAQ-13 can safely reach brain tumors, be tolerated by dogs receiving radiation therapy, and show early signs of effectiveness.


What happens in this study

  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical and neurologic examination, blood work, and diagnostic imaging


  1. Advanced brain imaging (MRI and CT scans) performed under general anesthesia


  1. Minimally invasive brain tumor biopsies performed at enrollment and after treatment


  1. Intravenous administration of an investigational drug (BAQ-13) twice weekly for 4 weeks


  1. Concurrent radiation therapy (standard of care)


  1. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample collection at specified time points


  1. Overnight hospitalization following biopsy procedures


  1. Follow-up visits, including in-hospital evaluations and telemedicine check-ins


  1. Completion of owner questionnaires to monitor quality of life and treatment effects


  1. End of Study: When your family is ready to elect humane euthanasia, your dog will return to UC Davis. A brief examination will be performed prior to humane euthanasia. Following your dog\u2019s death, a brain MRI will be performed, and they will undergo a routine necropsy. We will evaluate distribution of the drug in the brain, brain tumor, and vital organs (heart, lung, kidneys, liver). If your dog passes away or is euthanized elsewhere, the study team will arrange return to UC Davis for post-mortem evaluation.

"description": "Purpose of Study: Surgical removal is generally recommended as the first step in treatment of mast cell tumors; however, sometimes surgery is not possible due to the size or location of the tumor or due to financial limitations. In that situation, treatment with steroids, chemotherapy or targeted therapies such as Masitinib may be beneficial in controlling the disease. Preliminary studies of Masitinib in dogs showed that it caused tumor shrinkage in 50% of dogs with mast cell tumors and increased 1- and 2-year survival rates in dogs with nonresectable mast cell tumors compared to placebo. Based on this data, Masitinib has conditional approval by the FDA for treatment of non-resectable grade 2 or 3 mast cell tumors in dogs. The objective of the study is to evaluate the anti-cancer effects of Masitinib in comparison to a placebo in dogs with grade 2 or 3 mast cell tumors that have not been previously removed or treated with chemotherapy or radiation. If this study confirms these results, the drug will become fully approved. Contact: The Oncology Clinical Trial Coordinators via email (oncologyclinicaltrials@ucdavis.edu) or phone (530-752-0125 or 530-752-9759) Participation Requirements:Please Contact us for specific requirements Initial Evaluation for Participation: Please contact Oncologyclinicaltrials@ucdavis.edu Procedures: If your dog is enrolled, a small biopsy will be taken from the mast cell tumor to confirm grade and for additional testing. Your dog will then be randomly assigned to receive treatment with either Masitinib or a placebo with two-thirds of the dogs receiving Masitinib and one-third receiving placebo. You will not know whether you are giving the study drug or the placebo (even after you dog has completed the study). Your pet will come in every other week for examination, tumor measurement, blood work and imaging tests (x-rays and/or ultrasound) to check for cancer progression and/or side effects from the drug. No more than 1 tablespoon of blood will be drawn per visit. More invasive testing (fine needle aspiration) will only occur if your veterinarian is concerned about spread of the cancer or to monitor spread to a lymph node that has already occurred. Your dog cannot receive steroids or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs during the study period, but can receive medications to treat nausea, diarrhea, infection, itchiness, and pain if needed. Benefits: You are responsible for the initial consult visit fee at UCDavis. If you and your dog meet the inclusion/exclusion criteria, staging will be covered by study (Blood work, Biopsy, Bone Marrow Aspirates, Radiographs, Ultrasound) regardless if your dog qualifies. Although not all tumors will respond to Masitinib, it is possible that the drug may help control your dogs mast cell tumor. The information gathered from this study may help other dogs with mast cell tumors in the future by determining whether Masitinib is an effective treatment for non-resectable grade 2 or 3 mast cell tumors. In normal cells, PAK 4 is tightly regulated so that growth occurs in a normal ordered manner. It is now known that abnormalities occur in PAK4 in cancer cells that contribute to driving uncontrolled tumor growth. In some cells there are mutations in PAK4 that cause it to be turned on all the time, and in others its expression is very high causing the tumor cells to divide uncontrollably. Based on the role of PAK4 in cancer there has been great interest in developing inhibitors of this protein that can be used to treat tumors and possibly halt their growth. Karyopharm Therapeutics has developed a drug called KPT-9274 that is given orally and binds to PAK4, thereby blocking its ability to drive cell growth. The goal of this study is to determine if photodynamic therapy would be useful in treating dog and potentially human lung tumors. The steps of photodynamic therapy include injection of a photosensitizing agent into the blood. The drug is absorbed all over the body, but stays in cancer cells slightly longer than in normal cells. Two days after drug absorption, the tumor is exposed to a light source. Photosensitizer agents in the cells absorb the light and produce an active form of oxygen which destroys nearby cells. Patient Entry Criteria: Eligible patients include dogs having a single lung tumor greater than 2 centimeters in diameter. The patient will need to have a needle aspirate taken of the tumor which confirms a diagnosis of carcinoma prior to enrollment. Also recent chest radiographs, a complete blood count, a serum biochemistry panel, and a urinalysis are necessary prior to enrollment. The study is limited to dogs not having evidence of metastatic disease and who are in otherwise good health. What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? Each dog will receive an intravenous injection of a photosensitizing agent on Day 0. Two days later on Day 2, each dog will be anesthetized for a chest CT scan and additional outpatient procedures. Following the CT scan while still anesthetized, a bronchoscopy (a flexible camera placed inside the trachea and lung airway branches) will be combined with fluoroscopy (a version of real-time chest xray imaging) to deliver a lighted wire through the bronchoscope for temporary placement into the lung tumor of each dog. Just prior to the lighted wire placement, a second photosensitizing agent acid will be given either orally or intravenously. Once the lighted wire has been activated to stimulate photosensitizing drugs within the lung tumor to cause cell death, the wire and scope will be removed. Two days later on Day 4, each dog will be readmitted to the hospital for routine surgical removal of the lung tumor via traditional thoracic surgery. Reevaluation with the Clinical Trials team at Colorado State University will be expected at two weeks, four weeks, and six weeks after the traditional thoracic surgery. Your pet will experience side effects. Specifically, dogs will experience light sensitivity, or photosensitivity, following administration of the photosensitizing drugs. The light sensitivity is expected to last from two to six weeks, the estimated amount of time for the drugs to be eliminated from the body. It is anticipated the ears may be the most sensitive to side effect, and will be a barometer for overall photosensitivity, but any exposed or lightly haired area of the body is susceptible including the belly, mouth, and eye tissues. Any strong light, including indoor as well as sunlight, could affect photosensitivity. Thus dogs will need to be kept mostly indoors during the time period of about one month, until the drugs are metabolized. Use of sunscreen products will not be of benefit. Dogs will need to be protected against unrestricted outdoor sunlight exposure in the first month following treatment by being supervised on a leash long enough to allow for urinations and defecations. If the ears become red or show signs suggestive of a 'sun burn' while a dog is being quarantined indoors, then less use of bright indoor lights will be recommended to reduce exposure effects. Importantly, controlled light exposure is the key for metabolism of the photosensitizing agents. Standard of Care is defined as definitive surgery, being amputation of the affected limb, followed by 4 doses of intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy given on an every 21 day schedule. Carboplatin has been shown to safely and effectively improve survival in dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma for over 20 years. ALL dogs enrolled onto study will receive Standard of Care (SOC) therapy; however, through a randomization process, some dogs entered into study will also receive additional therapy with oral rapamycin. Rapamycin is a drug currently approved to induce immunosuppression in human patients receiving organ and bone marrow transplants. Early work with rapamycin suggests that this agent might also have anti-cancer properties by inhibiting (reducing the effects of) an important pathway in cancer progression known as mTOR. Preclinical studies of rapamycin in mice, as well as recent data using analogous drugs (rapalogs) in human patients, suggest that mTOR blockade might be effective in the treatment of several cancers. Study Objective This study will evaluate if orally administered rapamycin following SOC therapy improves long-term disease control in dogs with osteosarcoma. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: - Confirmed diagnosis of osteosarcoma - Primary appendicular osteosarcoma that is amenable to surgical removal via amputation (No evidence that the tumor has spread to the lung (metastasis) based upon physical exam, thoracic radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound). - ONLY newly diagnosed dogs are eligible with no prior therapy (conventional or metronomic chemotherapy, ionizing radiation, bisphosphonates) for osteosarcoma. - Dogs receiving analgesics including NSAIDs, gabapentin, tramadol, or other will be eligible for study inclusion. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To enroll in this study, you must sign informed consent allowing the surgical amputation of your dog's affected limb. Following amputation, your dog will return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital every 3 weeks for 15 weeks for evaluation. On weeks 3, 6, 9 and 12 your dog will receive a dose of carboplatin. Precautions should be taken against contact with your dog's urine or feces for 48 hours after carboplatin treatment. Blood work will be done on your dog prior to carboplatin administration. After completion of SOC therapy, and depending upon initial study randomization, you might be required to administer oral rapamycin (PO) at home for 4 months. The schedule for rapamycin administration will be daily on Monday-Thursday (4 days on), with a drug holiday on Friday, Saturday and Sunday (no dosing, 3 days off). This will allow us to determine if oral rapamycin can be safely administered chronically and will require serial collections of blood on scheduled reevaluations to allow for measurements of rapamycin within your dog's blood. Your dog will have a total of five 24-hour serial blood draws completed over the course of 4 months. At the end of the each study cycle (Day 25), your dog must return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital for reassessment and further blood collections. Purpose of Study: Standard therapy for dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma has long been amputation of the affected limb followed by chemotherapy to prevent the spread of cancer. With this form of treatment, survival times of dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma is on average about 10 to 12 months with little improvement in survival occurring over the past two decades. Rapamycin is a drug that potentially can inhibit an important pathway in cancer progression known as mTOR. The purpose of this study is to determine if adding the oral drug Rapamycin into the treatment protocol for dogs with osteosarcoma will be safe and improve efficacy of current standard therapies for osteosarcoma in dogs. There will be about 160 dogs taking part in this study that is enrolling dogs nationwide. Initial Evaluation for Participation: If you allow your dog to participate in this study, you will be responsible for the cost of the initial examination with the UC Davis Oncology Service as well as the cost of the screening diagnostic tests, which include a complete blood count (CBC), biochemical profile, urinalysis, chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound. Participation Requirements: Most of the exams, tests, and procedures you will have are part of the usual approach for your dogs treatment for osteosarcoma including amputation of the affected limb and carboplatin chemotherapy given once every three weeks for 4 doses followed by monitoring of chest x-rays once every two months. Week 1 evaluation - amputation Weeks 3, 6, 9 and 12 evaluation-blood work and carboplatin treatment (and chest x-rays at week 9) Week 15 evaluation-chest x-rays Every 8 weeks recheck chest x-rays-Some extra sample (tumor and blood) collections for dogs enrolled in both study groups will need to be taken if you take part in this study. Additionally, dogs enrolled in the Rapamycin Group will have extra visits required of them during the 4 months that they are receiving oral rapamycin and owners are expected to administer the oral rapamycin once daily Monday through Thursday. Benefits: Benefits of standard therapy include removal of the painful cancerous tumor in your dogs bone and delay of spread of cancer by providing chemotherapy with carboplatin. Once enrolled, the study will provide a $1000 hospital credit toward the cost of your dogs amputation and will provide the total cost of carboplatin chemotherapy and follow-up examination and diagnostics. For dogs enrolled in the Rapamycin Group, we cannot promise any benefits to your pet or other animals from your taking part in this clinical trial. Owner Responsibilities: Once enrolled in the clinical trial, you are responsible for scheduling and keeping all appointments needed for study participation and reporting any side effects of the treatment to your doctor in a timely manner. You will be responsible for the cost of amputation above and beyond the $1000 hospital credit provided by the study. You will also be responsible for any costs associated with management of side effects from the standard therapy portion of this study (amputation and carboplatin chemotherapy). All other study costs associated with study participation will be covered by the study. Multiple Institutions are participating For a complete list, go to: https://ccrod.cancer.gov/confluence/display/CCRCOPWeb/Current+Open+Trials Contact: The Oncology Clinical Trial Coordinators via email (oncologyclinicaltrials@ucdavis.edu) or phone (530-752-0125 or 530-752-9759)

Physiologically, dogs with relative upper airway obstruction exhibit increased inspiratory effort which can result in an increase in negative intrapleural and intraesophageal pressure. This, in turn, can lead to cranial motion of the stomach into the thoracic cavity during inspiration with subsequent gastresophageal reflux (GER) and hiatal herniation (HH). The effect of increases in inspiratory effort on GER and HH have been evaluated in people with asthma and it has been shown that asthmatics with some degree of airway obstruction had significantly lower esophageal sphincter pressures, greater esophageal acid exposure and more frequent reflux episodes than controls. In veterinary patients, in which chronic upper airway obstructions are a much more common clinical entity, an association between respiratory and gastroesophageal disease has long been hypothesized, especially in brachycephalic breeds. However, a direct causal relationship has never been established and objective documentation of the response to amelioration of the upper respiratory obstruction on the severity of GER and/or HH has never been thoroughly investigated. Despite the frequent concurrence of respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms in brachycephalic dog breeds the area has been the subject of very little investigation in the veterinary literature. This may, in part, be due to the difficulty in diagnosis of these pathologies in the past. In recent years better diagnostic tests for the diagnosis of the associated pathologies have become available. Contrast-enhanced videofluoroscopy has become the gold standard for diagnosis of a host of gastroesophageal disorders and has been established as the primary diagnostic assessment of GER and HH in the authors institution for several years. Lower esophageal pH evaluation using 24hr ambulatory monitoring is now available and has been shown in people to correlate well with GER disease. When the pH drops below a certain threshold (usually set at a pH of 4) an episode of gastric acid reflux has occurred. Twenty-four hour pH monitoring is used extensively in people for investigation of reflux-related symptoms that are refractory to proton-pump inhibitor therapy and can help to guide therapy in these patients. Impedance planimetry using the Endoflip device (Crospon Inc. Galway, Ireland) is a modality that provides real-time information on the dimensions and distensibility of the lower esophageal area in dogs. A balloon tipped catheter is passed down the esophagus and positioned across the lower esophageal area. Monitoring high-resolution manometry (HRM) allows accurate assessment of neuromuscular activity within the esophagus and esophageal sphincters using a probe incorporating 36 pressure sensors. The device allows the creation of spatiotemporal plots of esophageal pressure activity along the entire length of the esophagus and helps to elucidate the functional anatomy of the structures involved in HH. HRM has been evaluated for diagnosis of HH in humans and traditional water-based manometry has been evaluated for diagnosis of the condition in a canine model. These new diagnostic modalities will be used in addition to standardized client questionnaires filled out pre and post-operatively to evaluate the effect of palliation of the upper airway obstruction on the severity of HH. Procedures:Brachycephalic (short-nosed breeds) dogs suffer from relative upper airway obstruction which causes a decrease in pressure in the chest during inspiration which can lead to their upper stomach area being pulled into the chest (hiatal herniation). "description": "Horses with severe colic require surgery to correct intestinal obstruction, and it is this population of horses that requires the most intensive care to save their lives. Survival rates have continued to increase as equine anesthesia and surgery has progressively improved. This has shifted the emphasis of colic treatment to intensive medical care that is required before and particularly after surgery. There are a number of treatments that have become the standard of care for horses with severe colic, including intravenous fluids and anti-inflammatory medications, such as flunixin meglumine (Banamine). However, just as there have been advances in anesthesia and surgery, there have also been advances in medical therapy. One such advance has been the development of drugs called COX-2 inhibitors, which have an action similar to flunixin, but target inflammation much more specifically. Recent scientific discoveries have shown that the COX enzymes are responsible for beneficial functions, such as digestive and kidney health via COX-1, and detrimental functions, such as pain and inflammation via COX-2. Flunixin inhibits both COX enzymes, so it has benefits to horses with colic (pain relief and reduced inflammation) as well as side effects (stomach ulcers, kidney damage). We have recently discovered a new side effect of flunixin it slows down repair of the gut because it inhibits COX-1. However, since 2010, an intravenous COX-2 inhibitor has been released on the market specifically for horses called firocoxib (Equioxx). We have shown in research trials comparing flunixin and firocoxib that while both provided excellent levels of pain relief, flunixin reduced the rate at which the bowel could recover from colic-induced injury, whereas firocoxib allowed the bowel to recover more rapidly. We believe this may be a very important consideration when treating horses with surgical colic. To properly test this, we are proposing a multi-institutional clinical trial in which owners of colic patients going to surgery at NC State University, Michigan State University, or the University of Pennsylvania will have the option of enrolling their horse in a clinical trial in which flunixin or firocoxib will be given. The drug being used will be hidden from the veterinarians (they will know one of two anti-inflammatory drugs are being given). We will also give the drugs to horses in random order. This is all part of running a high level clinical trial, to make sure the results are as meaningful as possible. Clients will be given a small financial incentive to enroll their horses in this trial, and all other aspects of medical and surgical treatment will be kept the same. We will determine if one drug is advantageous over the other by measuring a comprehensive series of clinical measures (e.g., level of shock) as well as blood levels of bacterial toxins and markers of septic shock. The outcome will be a far greater understanding of the effects of both flunixin and firocoxib in horses with surgical colic, which we believe will help clinicians enhance their level of medical care in these critically ill horses.", "absolute_url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/the-study-of-optimal-non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory-drug-for-horses-with-severe-colic-545380/?ref=gallery", "tagline": null, "name": "The study of optimal non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug for horses with severe colic", "visible_sc_items": [{"id": 832, "tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type", "show_as_attribute_on_card": false, "icon": null}, {"id": 665, "tag_path": "primary-field-19_equine-surgery-16_alimentary-gastrointestinal-168", "label": "Alimentary - The needed dilution of allergen extract used in an IDT is defined by determining threshold concentrations (TCs) in normal non-allergic dogs. An allergen extract used at too dilute of a concentration may predispose to false negative skin test reactions, whereas an allergen extract used in too high of a concentration may cause false positive skin test reactions. Initial evaluation of TCs for finding the exact concentration of allergens that should be used in an IDT are determined by comparing skin test reactivity with serial dilutions of allergen extract in non-hypersensitive patients. Currently, there are no allergenic extracts that have been standardized for use in veterinary medicine. As reference standards are not established there is great variation in potency and reactivity both among lots of allergen extracts and between suppliers. This trial will establish threshold concentrations of allergens from a new veterinary allergen supplier. central hypothesis is that a novel ventral cervical fusion technique requiring minimal cervical disk removal and utilizing a combination of PEEK (poly-ether-ether-ketone) intervertebral spacers along with stabilizing pedicle screws and connecting rods will be a safe and effective way to fuse a cervical interdisk space in a horse within 6 - 12 months post-surgery. We predict that these implants utilized for cervical fusion will maintain complete stabilization and improve clinical signs of ataxia throughout the study period. Specific Aims- 1) To determine if a novel cervical fusion technique requiring minimal cervical disk removal and utilizing a combination of PEEK (poly-ether-ether-ketone) interbody spacers along with stabilizing pedicle screws and connecting rods will be a safe and effective way to achieve complete and successful cervical fusion within 12 months of surgery. Background and Significance: Neurological gait deficits resulting from cervical vertebral disease in horses is not uncommon. These deficits lead to decreased athletic abilities at a minimum, with recumbency and even death in severe cases. Cervical vertebral compressive myelopathy (CVCM) results in intermittent or continuous extradural compression of the spinal cord. Clinical signs include symmetrical ataxia along with paresis and spasticity that is often worse in the hindlimbs. CVCM is the leading cause of non-infectious spinal cord ataxia in the horse. It is estimated that it effects approximately 2% of Thoroughbred horses resulting in significant economic losses and welfare concerns. Most recently, a multicenter case-control study reported that 173 of 263 (66%) of CVCM cases were euthanized before discharge from the hospital. Many of the horses affected are young, with early clinical signs noted between 1 and 2 years of age. However, older horses are also affected as a result of osteoarthritis of the caudal cervical articular process joints. CVCM leads to Wallerian degeneration, malacia and fibrosis at locations of cord compression and demyelination of white matter. Unfortunately, these neurologic lesions often result in a horse that is not suitable for its intended purpose, leading to euthanasia in many scenarios. While the cause of CVCM has not been completely identified, multiple factors are believed to contribute, including rapid growth, trauma, nutrition, and abnormal biomechanical forces. There is currently no evidence confirming that CVCM is heritable. Both medical and surgical treatments are performed for the treatment of CVCM. Conservative treatments consist of nutritional restrictions of carbohydrates and proteins, systemic anti-inflammatory drugs, along with local therapeutics to the cervical vertebral articulations. A recent retrospective study evaluating racing records following conservative management of cervical vertebral malformations showed a prognosis for racing of 30%. Surgical treatment consists either of cervical fusion resulting in improved stability or dorsal laminectomy resulting in reduced spinal cord compression. Neurologic function was improved in 56 of 73 horses (77%) that underwent surgery. However, only 23% of surgically treated horses went on to either train of return to racing. The most commonly performed surgical procedure is cervical fusion with a Bagby Basket or Kerf-Cut Cylinder through a ventral approach. Overall, the success rate for surgeons utilizing this technique is approximately 60%. This technique relies solely on compression for stabilization, resulting in micromotion, a large amount of unwanted bone formation, and slow fusion rates (approximately 1 year). This technique also leaves very little room for error and can result in numerous catastrophic complications including ventral migration of the implant and vertebral fractures. The current procedure carries a reported fatality rate of 9%. More recently, a few studies have evaluated the use of a ventral locking plate to provide stabilization for cervical fusion. This technique has not been thoroughly evaluated clinically, but implant failure has been reported in animals as young as 3-months, making the technique questionable on the basis of biomechanical strength. In the dog, cervical stabilization is typically performed with a Steinman pin and bone cement technique with positive post-operative outcomes in about 80-90% of patients. In people, anterior discectomy and fusion is the mainstay for treatment of patients with cervical spondolytic myelopathy and some cases of discogenic radiculopathy. Spinal fusions in people are very common with over 300,000 procedures performed annually. A variety of techniques have been evaluated for fusion, including the use of plates and pedicle screws and rods in conjunction with bone allograft and autograft, intervertebral cement, or interbody cages. Recently, much research has been performed to develop an ideal interbody cage that will allow rapid growth of bone across the disc space in order to rapidly achieve full fusion. Poly-ether-ether-ketone (PEEK) cage is an interbody fusion device that has replaced allografts and metal implants such as the Bagby Basket and Kerf-Cut cylinder in human spinal fusion. PEEK is biomechanically similar to native bone, highly impervious to degredation or damage, biocompatible and radiolucent. The combination of a PEEK interbody fusion device and pedicle screws with connecting rods is currently the gold standard technique for lumbar fusion in people. The horse, in comparison to the human and the dog, offers a unique set of challenges due to their size and limitations in our ability to completely control post-operative motion, necessitating an extremely stable construct for cervical fusion. The Surgical Research Laboratory at Colorado State University has extensive expertise in the area of spinal fusion, performing over 3,500 cervical or lumbar fusions in sheep to evaluate novel implants, devices and biomaterials. From our extensive preclinical experience with spinal fusion, we feel that that stabilizing techniques and implants utilized in humans can successfully be translated to the horse for cervical fusion. The advantages of the PEEK device with pedicle screws and connecting rods are numerous. These implants are easy to use and readily available. Unlike the current equine techniques, error is less likely to result in serious complications. Less disk space removal is required and immediate stability is provided in compression and tension. The combination of both factors is likely to result in improved fusion rates as early as 4-6 months based on our previous experience in spinal fusion in sheep. To date the technique has been successfully employed in at least 10 horses. Research Design and Methods: This protocol has been approved by the Colorado State University Animal Care and Use Committee. Horses undergo an extensive neurologic evaluation including objective gait analysis prior to enrollment. Also horses undergo imaging including cervical radiographs, myelography, and CT to achieve a diagnosis of CVCM. Horses will undergo ventral cervical stabilization for cervical fusion utilizing a PEEK interbody fusion device with pedicle screws and connecting rods. The horse will be placed under general anesthesia in dorsal recumbency with the neck extended in full flexion. Fluoroscopy will be utilized throughout the procedure to ensure that the compressied site(s) is/are identified and that implants are accurately placed in the correct location. A ventral midline approach to the cervical spine is used similar to the published Kerf-Cut cylinder technique. The ventral aspect is exposed and the disk space is identified. A small section of keel will be removed and used as a bone graft. Using a Midas-Rex neurologic drill, a bone window is created through the keel and into the disk space to a depth of approximately 35mm. The bone window will accommodate a 30mm length x 24 mm depth x 14mm height PEEK intervertebral fusion device. The bone removed from the keel will be broken into small pieces and placed into the openings of the PEEK device to act a bone graft. The device will be impacted into the space and in close contact to the endplate. Once the PEEK device is in place, a 3.2mm unicortical hole will be drilled into the left and right side close to the disk space and approximately 5cm apart. A 4.5mm x 30mm polyaxial pedicle screw will be screwed into each hole to an appropriate depth under fluoroscopic guidance. Once the pedicle screws are in place, a 5.0mm connecting rod cut to the appropriate size will span the disk space and placed into the head of the polyaxial pedicle screws. Your pets clinician will discuss standard treatment and clinical trial options with you. It is your decision whether or not you want your pet to participate in a clinical trial. You may discuss your pets participation with your family and your pets veterinarian. If you have any questions, please ask your pets clinician for additional information. Why is this clinical trial being conducted? Gliomas in dogs are known to be a very aggressive cancer with relatively short survival times despite our best efforts at treatment. Because of this, we are always looking for new ways to treat this disease. Many new cancer treatments are aimed at activating the patients own immune system (called immunotherapy) to potentially make it more effective at fighting off the cancer. One form of immunotherapy is tumor vaccines. This vaccine was developed in the Dow Laboratory, and targets the cancer stem cells, which are the precursor cells that then migrate and mature into active tumor cells with appropriate biochemical signals. These cancer stem cells are thought to be responsible for the inevitable recurrence of gliomas. These cells are present in the subventricular zone of the brain, and as such are not accessible for resection with the primary tumor. As these precursor cells are not in active division and thus are resistant to chemotherapy and radiation therapy, immunotherapies are likely the key to achieving improved outcomes for gliomas. A successful vaccine that targets these cancer stem cells would be invaluable. The goal of this study is to evaluate preliminary tumor response to vaccination as well as vaccine tolerability. Which patients are eligible to participate in this clinical trial? To be eligible for this study, dogs must have a brain tumor that is presumed to be in the glioma family based on MRI characteristics. The results of the study will improve the diagnostic evaluation of pulmonary hypertension (PH) in dogs and our understanding of dogs with pre-clinical CVD, providing for the first time important data on cardiac function. Eligibility Dogs with mitral valve disease (also known as endocardiosis) that have: o an enlarged heart on chest X-ray o mitral valve disease confirmed by cardiac ultrasound (echocardiography) o tricuspid regurgitation (backflow through the tricuspid valve) identified by cardiac ultrasound (echocardiography) My dog is being treated for heart disease, can he be enrolled in the study? Exclusion Criteria Dogs with mitral valve disease that do not have an enlarged heart Dogs that have other significant diseases such as kidney disease Dogs weighting less than 5 kg (11 pounds) Study Design Dogs will undergo standard echocardiographic examination to establish baseline measurements. Avoidance of implicated allergens is impractical or impossible in most cases. These approaches to treatment are not entirely reliable, have potential for adverse reactions, or they come with significant financ ial burden.
